newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seeks details on NATO force plan.
newsitem.headline: Russia seeks details on NATO force plan.

text.p: Russian leaders kept silent on Wednesday on U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's proposal to create a joint Russian-NATO brigade, saying they needed more details before responding.

But the idea, part of measures designed to reassure Moscow over NATO's plans to expand towards Russia's doorstep, was greeted with mistrust by communists and nationalists who accused Albright of trying "to cheat Orthodox Christians".

Albright has a chance to spell out the proposal, which she announced in Brussels on Tuesday, during talks in Moscow on Thursday and Friday in which she will try to ease Russian fears over the Western defence alliance's eastward expansion plans.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov responded cautiously, telling Reuters: "I have not heard about it from her (Albright). I heard about it through the press, so I will refrain from any comment."
But Deputy Foreign Minister Nikolai Afanasyevsky said Moscow would welcome more details. "This would be of interest to us," he was quoted as saying by Interfax news agency.
Itar-Tass news agency and Interfax also quoted an unnamed general at the headquarters of the armed forces' general staff as saying Moscow would consider Albright's proposal.

"If this is some kind of screen for Europe's defence from who know's what, then it is unacceptable. It is another matter if this joint brigade carries out peacekeeping functions like those of the multinational forces in Bosnia," the general said.
"Russia is ready to examine the proposal," Tass said.
Albright outlined the proposal to NATO foreign ministers during a tour of Europe which will take her to Russia for a visit culminating in talks with President Boris Yeltsin.

She has indicated that the brigade would primarily be a peacekeeping force, complementing the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's vision of a joint alliance-Russia body that would promote regular dialogue on security issues.

Opposition to NATO's plans to take in former Warsaw Pact member states is one of the few things on which Yeltsin and his political opponents agree. They say it threatens Russia's security and would create divisions in Europe.

Communists and nationalists wasted little time in pouring scorn on Albright's proposal. Communist Alexei Podberyozkin criticised Russia's participation in the peacekeeping force in Bosnia but said the new brigade would be a bigger mistake.
"Our country's joint participation with NATO in a brigade under who knows whose command would be even worse," he said.
Nationalist leader Vladimir Zhirinovsky dismissed the idea in comments to Interfax, suggesting Moscow should respond to NATO's eastward enlargement by advancing westwards.
"Madam Albright is happy that Russia is dying," he said.
Albert Makashov, a communist retired general who serves on the lower house of parliament's defence committee, said: "The West, as always, is cheating Orthodox Christians."

More liberal members of parliament said the proposal was worthy of consideration if it was a step towards closer cooperation but would not be acceptable it it were an empty gesture intended to sweeten Russia over NATO expansion.

"Contacts with NATO should in principle be maintained because any contacts provide a chance to feel what is going on in NATO from inside," said Eduard Vorobyov, a retired general who is also a member of the parliamentary defence comittee.
